group: Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk
question:
Patient note:
A 74-year-old man checked in this morning to the pre-operative assessment unit four days before an elective right total knee arthroplasty for end-stage medial compartment osteoarthritis that has limited his golfing and stair climbing despite optimized physical therapy and two serial corticosteroid injections; the orthopedic team anticipates a midline parapatellar approach, a tourniquet time of approximately seventy minutes, estimated blood loss under 300 mL, and postoperative transfer to the orthopedic ward with planned discharge on postoperative day two once ambulation with a walker and adequate pain control are demonstrated. He parked on the rooftop level of the visitor garage, descended the full flight of concrete stairs rather than waiting for the elevator, and walked the two-hundred-meter corridor to registration at a measured pace, reporting only mild right knee stiffness but no shortness of breath or chest discomfort. At home he mows his own lawn with a riding mower, carries two grocery bags up a single flight, and can complete twelve minutes on a stationary bicycle set to moderate resistance without pauses, though he avoids hills because the prosthetic knee brace chafes. Sixteen years ago he presented to an outside emergency department with crushing substernal pressure that radiated to the left arm; emergent coronary angiography showed a proximal left anterior descending artery occlusion successfully treated with a drug-eluting stent. He completed cardiac rehabilitation, has remained pain-free on exertion, and sees cardiology annually; a nuclear stress study performed eight months ago achieved nine metabolic equivalents and revealed no perfusion defect or ischemic electrocardiographic changes. Current cardiovascular medications include aspirin 81 mg daily, clopidogrel 75 mg that will be paused five days before surgery per cardiology, high-intensity atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, and metoprolol succinate 25 mg each morning; blood pressure logs submitted through his patient portal average 124/68 mm Hg. He was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes during a life-insurance examination ten years ago; glycemic control has been maintained with metformin 1000 mg twice daily, most recent hemoglobin A1c 6.7 % and self-monitored fasting capillary glucose 100–120 mg/dL. He has never required injectable glucose-lowering therapy. There is no personal history of transient neurologic deficits, carotid procedures, or seizure disorders. Respiratory history is limited to well-controlled mild intermittent asthma requiring albuterol inhalation less than monthly; pulmonary function testing last year was normal. Renal stones, chronic liver disease, connective tissue disease, or known heart-valve abnormalities are denied. Prior surgeries include laparoscopic sigmoid colectomy for diverticulitis at age 60, left cataract extraction at 71, and Mohs excision of a basal cell carcinoma on the forearm without incident. He quit cigarette smoking twenty-five years ago after a 20-pack-year exposure, drinks a single glass of red wine with Sunday dinner, and denies recreational drug use. Both parents lived into their late eighties; his father underwent coronary bypass at 77, and his mother had osteoporosis but no vascular events. Review of systems today is negative for fever, chills, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, pedal edema, palpitations, syncope, claudication, abdominal pain, urinary frequency, or unintended weight change. After five minutes of seated rest, vital signs obtained on the right arm showed blood pressure 122/70 mm Hg, regular pulse 64 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, oral temperature 36.5 °C, and oxygen saturation 97 % on ambient air; height is 178 cm, weight 93 kg, body-mass index 29.3 kg/m². He appears comfortable and euvolemic. Jugular venous pulsation is less than 3 cm above the sternal angle at 45°, carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruit, and the point of maximal impulse is localized in the fifth intercostal space mid-clavicular line without displacement. Cardiac auscultation reveals a crisp S1 and physiologically split S2, no gallop, and a soft midsystolic murmur at the left sternal border thought secondary to flow across a sclerotic aortic valve; no pericardial rub is heard. Lungs are clear to percussion and auscultation with good diaphragmatic excursion. Abdomen is flat, nontender, and without organomegaly; surgical scars from the prior colectomy are well healed. The right knee demonstrates a 10-degree flexion contracture, crepitus on passive motion, and bony enlargement along the medial joint line; distal pulses are 2 + and symmetric. Neurologic screening shows full orientation, 5/5 strength, intact sensation to light touch and vibration, and a stable tandem gait once the knee is braced. Pre-operative laboratories drawn one hour before examination reveal hemoglobin 13.7 g/dL, hematocrit 41 %, white blood cell count 6.1 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 235 × 10⁹/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, chloride 104 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 22 mg/dL, and a serum creatinine of 1.63 mg/dL, corresponding to an estimated glomerular filtration rate of approximately 48 mL/min/1.73 m². Fasting glucose in the same specimen is 116 mg/dL; liver enzymes and international normalized ratio are within reference limits. Twelve-lead electrocardiography obtained in clinic demonstrates normal sinus rhythm at 62 beats/min, Q waves in V1–V3 consistent with prior infarction, and no acute ST-segment changes compared with a tracing six months earlier. Upright postero-anterior chest radiography displays a normal cardiomediastinal silhouette and clear lung fields. Airway evaluation yields Mallampati class II, inter-incisor distance 4 cm, thyromental distance 6 cm, and full cervical extension without loose teeth. The anesthetic plan is to continue beta-blocker, statin, and metformin through the morning of surgery, withhold clopidogrel as scheduled, employ regional spinal anesthesia supplemented by light sedation to limit systemic opioids, place a pneumatic tourniquet for blood-sparing, administer tranexamic acid, and utilize multimodal postoperative analgesia including a femoral nerve block. Sequential compression devices will be applied intraoperatively and chemical thromboprophylaxis initiated twelve hours after spinal needle removal. After discussion of potential cardiac, renal, thromboembolic, infectious, and neurologic risks, the patient accurately repeated medication timing and fasting instructions and voiced readiness to proceed with joint replacement to regain pain-free ambulation.

Question: What is the patient's score of the Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI) assigns one point for each of six preoperative risk factors:
- High-risk surgery (intraperitoneal, intrathoracic, or suprainguinal vascular): planned knee arthroplasty is orthopedic → 0.
- Ischemic heart disease: prior LAD infarction treated with a stent, with residual infarct Q waves → 1. A negative recent stress test does not erase this history.
- Heart failure: no history or clinical evidence → 0.
- Cerebrovascular disease: no prior stroke or TIA reported → 0.
- Preoperative insulin treatment: diabetes is managed with metformin alone → 0.
- Serum creatinine >2.0 mg/dL: preoperative value 1.63 mg/dL → 0.
Total = 0 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 1.
Final answer: 1
